source: Byrne (1989) Suppressing valid inferences with conditionals (numbers as tabulated in Dietz Saldanha and Kakas 2020)
finding: Adding a second conditional that names an extra requirement made people withdraw a valid modus ponens conclusion. Adding an alternative-cause conditional did not.
numbers: Modus ponens (she studies late in library): simple 96%, alternative premise 96%, additional-requirement premise 38%. Modus tollens: 92%, 96%, 33%. Denying the antecedent: 46%, 4%, 63%. Affirming the consequent: 71%, 13%, 54%. Three between-group conditions; group sizes not in the secondary source.
limits: Original paper not opened; figures read from a later paper's table. Closed answer options (see b03).
agent_relevance: A default rule can lose force when a salient missing condition is named. This is the human version of doubt on a signal. The signal is the disabling condition, not a schedule.

source: Dieussaert, Schaeken, Schroyens and d'Ydewalle (2000) Strategies during complex conditional inferences, experiment 2 (figures as tabulated in Dietz Saldanha and Kakas 2020)
finding: The suppression effect replicated in direction but was smaller than in Byrne. The baseline was also lower.
numbers: Modus ponens: simple 88%, alternative 93%, additional 60% (Byrne: 96, 96, 38). Modus tollens conclusion 'no essay' given 'no library': 69% (simple) and 44% (alternative) versus 92% and 96% in Byrne. Denying the antecedent: 49%, 22%, 49%.
limits: Secondary source only. The modus ponens drop is 28 points here versus 58 points in Byrne. Answer procedure and sampling differ.
agent_relevance: Expect a partial, size-variable effect of a named disabler. Do not assume a fixed drop of confidence when a defeater is mentioned.

source: Trehan, Laloi, Borensztajn, van Hoolwerff, Moas (2005) The Suppression Task Revisited (UvA course paper)
finding: With open answers instead of Byrne's fixed options, suppression mostly changed form. Most people reasoned with closed-world logic plus strengthening (reading if p then q as also only if).
numbers: N=10 adults, no logic background. Modus ponens: simple 100%, alternative 100%, additional 40% (Byrne 38%). Modus tollens additional: 100% valid-type answers versus 33% in Byrne, because maybe-answers counted as suppression in Byrne. Per subject: 5 mainly closed-world with strengthening, 2 as a minor tendency, 1 classical logic, 0 mainly probabilistic.
limits: Tiny N, course paper, not peer reviewed, answers coded by the authors. Shows an answer-format boundary, not a precise effect size.
agent_relevance: How the exception is represented decides what is withdrawn. Our lesson store should record the exception as an explicit condition on the rule, not only as lower confidence.

source: Knauff and Gazzo Castaneda (2026) Reasoning beyond clicks: counterexamples and probabilities in conditional reasoning (Memory and Cognition 54)
finding: With free-text answers, people often gave certain conclusions. When unsure, they cited concrete counterexamples more than probabilities. Graded rating scales may hide this (probabilistic masking).
numbers: Exp 1 N=20, Exp 2 N=37, over 1,300 responses, inter-rater agreement 97.3% and 98.3%. Exp 1 modus ponens: certain 30.9%, counterexample 45.0%, probability 24.2%; affirming the consequent 28.3%, 38.8%, 32.9%. Exp 2 modus ponens 28.0%, 45.6%, 26.4%; affirming the consequent 33.3%, 46.2%, 20.5%. About 30% certain throughout. A pilot with N=52 rated 48 conditionals; chosen high items about 88%, low items about 51-54%.
limits: Small, young samples recruited online, psychology-trained people excluded. Not preregistered. Only two inference types.
agent_relevance: Supports modelling doubt as a specific counterexample came to mind (default plus exception), not as a smooth probability. Matches a rule-with-exception memory item.

source: Schroyens, Fleerackers and Maes (2010) General aptitude and the assumption of truth in reasoning about probable but false conditionals
finding: Known counterexamples lower confidence in valid arguments less than in invalid ones. People seem to set aside background exceptions when asked to assume the premise. Higher general ability showed only a weak tendency to do this more.
numbers: Exp 1 N=117 (100 kept after a Raven split: low 32, medium 41, high 27); Exp 2 N=245. Few vs many counterexamples: valid arguments .831 vs .644 (d=.187); invalid .811 vs .486 (d=.325); interaction F(1,97)=49.2. Aptitude x validity F(2,97)=2.8, p=.063, not significant. Logic index vs ability r=.135, p=.182.
limits: Certainty ratings, not retraction. Exp 2 details not read beyond the abstract. Aptitude effect marginal in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Instruction framing matters: assume the rule suppresses exception search; check what could go wrong raises it. Make the framing explicit in the Revise slot.

source: Lopez-Astorga, Ragni and Johnson-Laird (2022) The probability of conditionals: a review (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 29)
finding: A review of the rival view that the probability of a conditional equals the conditional probability (the Equation). Intuitive estimates often equal p(A and C). Deliberate ones fit the Equation. The Equation seems to hold mainly when p(A) is reasonably high.
numbers: No pooled effect size in the passages read. Cites Skovgaard-Olsen et al. (2019) for the p(A) boundary.
limits: Review of conditionals, not of default logic as such. Abstract and introduction read in full, the experiment tables were not.
agent_relevance: Probability logic is the main rival to default logic. Human data rarely separate them, so do not claim a default-logic mechanism from human data alone.

source: Dietz Saldanha and Kakas (2020) Cognitive Argumentation and the Suppression Task
finding: A preference-based argumentation model explains Byrne's twelve cases and the minority answers. Part of the spread comes from reasoning in prediction mode versus explanation mode.
numbers: Modus tollens case: above 90% in Byrne groups I and II, only 69% in the Dieussaert replication. The model predicts possible versus definite conclusions and matches the 30-70% minority answers.
limits: Model fitted to published group percentages, not new data. The credulous versus skeptical split is a modelling choice.
agent_relevance: Gives a runnable rule: prefer the more specific or later argument, keep rival conclusions as possible. A template for the S5 retract step.

source: Leidinger, van Rooij and Shutova (2024) Are LLMs classical or nonmonotonic reasoners? Lessons from generics (ACL short)
finding: Seven open 7B-13B LLMs lower their agreement with a generic after an exception, as a nonmonotonic reasoner would. But they also drop for supporting and irrelevant exemplars.
numbers: Datasets: GEN-comm 650 generics, about 19,000 exemplars; GEN-abs 260 pairs. An exception lowers agreement for all models on both datasets (Wilcoxon p=0.01); agreement falls to 0% for Llama-2, Mixtral, Starling, WizardLM on GEN-abs. Supporting exemplar: only Mistral, OpenHermes, WizardLM stay above 90% on GEN-abs; Mixtral below 10%. Random exemplar: below 50% for Llama-2, Mistral, Mixtral, Zephyr (GEN-comm) and below 20% for five models (GEN-abs). OpenHermes stays above 85% on both.
limits: Temperature 0, yes/no answers, three phrasings by majority vote. Chain-of-thought and an alternative template gave similar results. English only. Small older models.
agent_relevance: A drop after an exception is not proof of defeasible reasoning: the same drop follows irrelevant text. This is the reason for G1: only revise when a code check ties the new item to the rule.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) Generics and Default Reasoning in Large Language Models: overall results
finding: 28 LLMs on 20 defeasible patterns. Frontier models do well on the uncontroversial ones. Rank is not tied to size.
numbers: 15 uncontroversial patterns, zero-shot, temperature 0: Claude 3 Opus and 3.5 Sonnet 96%; GPT-4 (0613) 93.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 92.7%; Gemma 2 9B 92%; GPT-4o (Aug) 91%; Llama 3.1 70B 85%; Mistral 7B and Mixtral 58%; Code Llama 34B 19%. Chance is 50%. Eleven models scored 78-89%, 7 near chance, 3 below chance. Gemma 2 9B beat 27B; Gemini Flash beat Pro.
limits: Scored against expert judgments from the literature, not human data. Models are 2023-2024 vintage.
agent_relevance: Plain default patterns (modus ponens, irrelevant facts) are solved by strong models. The risk is the edge cases, not the basic rule.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) chain-of-thought result
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought often lowered accuracy on default reasoning in models that were already good.
numbers: Mean drop -11.14 points (SD 15.74) among models above 75% zero-shot, temperature 0. Claude 3 Sonnet down more than 16; GPT-4 (0613) -12.62; Gemini 1.5 Flash -18.77; Claude 3.5 Sonnet -0.33. GPT-4o (May) +17.44, GPT-4o (Aug) +4.98. Code Llama 34B rose from 6.48% to above 62%. Error pattern: treating the generic as a universal and the exception as a counterexample.
limits: Zero-shot CoT only; sign differs by model. Manual error analysis covered three models.
agent_relevance: Do not add a reasoning pass to default inferences by habit. Long reasoning can turn usually into always. Matches our measured cost of forced doubt.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) few-shot and wording results
finding: Few-shot examples help weak models and do little or harm for strong ones. Small prompt changes can break scores.
numbers: Few-shot gains: Llama 2 Chat 7B +28.74; Claude 3 Haiku +25.08; GPT-4o (May) +16.27; Claude 3 Opus -6.81. Wording variants of the basic pattern correlate with the base prompt at 0.99, 0.99, 0.88 but only 0.54, 0.47, 0.43, and -0.05 for the worst.
limits: 28 models; per-pattern N is small (about 20 instances).
agent_relevance: State the rule and exception in one fixed format in the schema. Free wording is a hidden variable.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) defeasible versus deductive wording; generics read as universals
finding: Models that accept a defeasible inference also tend to call it deductively valid. They do not separate usually from always.
numbers: Across 28 models and 8 patterns, accuracy on the defeasible wording was negatively correlated with accuracy on the deductively-follows wording: r below -0.6 in 6 of 8 patterns (all p<.01). Mean accuracy for defeasible modus ponens 80.5% versus 30.1% on the deductive wording; for defeasible modus tollens 80.3% versus 25.1%. Overall r=-0.647.
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction; values read as printed. Only one pattern (defeasible defeat modus ponens) showed the expected positive correlation (r=0.90).
agent_relevance: LLMs may treat a default as a strict rule. Store defaults with an explicit defeasible tag and let code, not the model, apply retraction.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) irrelevance, premise order, argument length
finding: Top models ignore irrelevant facts, irrelevant defaults and exceptional individuals. Premise order helps some models and hurts others.
numbers: Basic default reasoning: GPT-4o (May) at chance, Gemini 1.5 Pro significantly below chance. Fact irrelevance: Claude 3 Haiku and Mistral 7B 75% zero-shot; GPT-3.5 (1106), Haiku, Llama Chat 7B rose from 75% to 100% few-shot. Specific premise first helped zero-shot defeasible modus ponens; GPT-4 Turbo (1106) fell below chance with that order on modus tollens. Arguments above 3 premises did not lower scores for models over 90%.
limits: Per-model effects are idiosyncratic. No inferential statistics for order effects.
agent_relevance: Put the specific case before the general rule in the retract prompt, after testing it on our own model.

source: Ishay and Lee (2026) LLMs as ASP Programmers: Self-Correction Enables Task-Agnostic Nonmonotonic Reasoning
finding: Letting an LLM write Answer Set Programs and fix them from solver errors beats the same LLMs answering directly on a default-reasoning set.
numbers: MultiLogicNMR (200 problems): baseline LLMs 59.0% skeptical and 52.9% credulous; LLM+ASP 90.5% and 81.0%; Gemini 2.5 Pro+ASP 100% skeptical. Average over six benchmarks 78.0% versus 51.3% baseline. Self-revision raised the average from 54.6% to 78.0%. Syntax errors fell from 360 to 18 cases with revisions. A reference guide raised accuracy from 61.4% to 70.0%; a compact guide beat verbose documentation (context rot).
limits: Four reasoning models (Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash, o4-mini, DeepSeek R1-0528); DeepSeek V3, non-reasoning, reached only 45.0%. 200 sampled problems per benchmark. Same group as earlier STAR work, so not independent.
agent_relevance: Strong support for the schema split: the model writes rules, code runs them. Default negation in a solver is a cheap, exact retract rule. Feed solver errors back, as G2 says.

source: Ishay and Lee (2026) LLM+ASP versus LLM+SMT and BoardgameQA saturation
finding: A monotonic solver (SMT) did no better than chance on nonmonotonic items. On BoardgameQA, plain reasoning models are now strong, so ASP added nothing there.
numbers: MultiLogicNMR: LLM+ASP 92.9% skeptical, 84.3% credulous; LLM+SMT 35.8% and 35.0% (chance 33.3%). BoardgameQA: LLM+ASP 82.1% vs LLM+SMT 60.1%; plain reasoning models 84.7% (LLM+ASP overall 82.4%; 92.0% vs 88.0% among reasoning models only). Constraint tasks went the other way: ZL-XL SMT 84.0% vs ASP 75.2%.
limits: The authors suspect BoardgameQA (2023) is in training data and that its explicit priorities allow pattern learning. 200-problem samples.
agent_relevance: Pick the tool by task: ASP-style defaults for exceptions, SMT for constraints. Plain reasoning models may already handle explicit-priority conflicts.

source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench: systematic evaluation of logical reasoning of LLMs (non-monotonic part)
finding: Non-monotonic rules from Lifschitz's list (default reasoning, irrelevant information, several defaults, disabled default, priorities) are hard for LLMs, hardest with several defaults and open domains.
numbers: Boolean QA, non-monotonic average accuracy, Yes-label / No-label (five models, order inferred): Llama-2 57.8/43.7, Mistral 71.0/67.5, Gemini-Pro 67.8/69.7, ChatGPT 61.5/65.5, GPT-4 74.4/84.8. Multiple choice, non-monotonic average: GPT-4 68.96; several-defaults item 55.0 and open-domain item 45.0 for GPT-4. Human accuracy on non-monotonic items 72.22% (first column of Table 8; column labels lost in extraction).
limits: Model order inferred from the text (GPT-4 and ChatGPT identified). Chain-of-thought prompts averaged over three. Synthetic template items.
agent_relevance: Weak spots to test on our own agent: several defaults at once, priorities, disabled defaults. Humans were not perfect either (about 72%).

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: reasoning with contradictory information
finding: Conflicts with rule preferences make language-model reasoning much harder. Few-shot pretrained models did not resolve conflicts out of the box. Fine-tuning helped but stayed poor.
numbers: 1000 train, 500 validation, 1000 test per variant; balanced labels, majority baseline 33%. Accuracy fell monotonically with conflict rate (0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8); BERT was above chance with none or low conflict and near chance at medium and high. Few-shot PaLM 540B beat 62B but was poor at every depth. The conflict type where the rule must be shown not to fire was harder than the type where it can be ignored. Proof checks showed few-shot models fail at conflict resolution even when the label is right.
limits: Exact accuracies appear only in figures, which were not read. 2023 models; later reasoning models score about 85% (see Ishay and Lee).
agent_relevance: A good test set for the Revise step: vary conflict rate and preference type.

source: Rudinger et al. (2020) Thinking Like a Skeptic: Defeasible Inference in Natural Language (delta-NLI)
finding: Strengtheners and weakeners of an inference can be collected at scale. A fine-tuned RoBERTa nearly matches humans on classification, but part of the score comes from artifacts.
numbers: Test accuracy (premise, hypothesis, update): delta-SNLI RoBERTa 81.6 vs human 83.6 vs majority 50.3; delta-ATOMIC 78.3 vs 78.2 vs 50.5; delta-SOCIAL 86.2 vs 87.6 vs 51.6. Update only: 65.1, 65.2, 71.6. Without the premise: 79.7 (SNLI) and 77.7 (ATOMIC). Validation agreement Krippendorff alpha 0.62, 0.67, 0.69. 230 crowd workers qualified.
limits: Hypothesis-plus-update baselines are strong, so benchmark gains overstate defeasible reasoning. In the generation task, best systems made a valid update up to 68% of the time.
agent_relevance: A model can often tell weakener from strengthener from the update text alone. In our setting code must tie the update to the specific rule used.

source: Madaan et al. (2021) Think about it! Improving defeasible reasoning by first modeling the question scenario (CURIOUS)
finding: Generating an inference graph of influences before judging a weakener or strengthener raised accuracy on three defeasible datasets.
numbers: delta-ATOMIC 80.2 vs 78.8 (strong end-to-end baseline) vs 78.3 previous best; delta-SNLI 85.6 vs 82.2 vs 81.6; delta-SOCIAL 88.6 vs 86.7 vs 86.2. Gains over the baseline: 1.4, 3.4, 1.9 points (marked significant).
limits: Small gains; trained 2021 model.
agent_relevance: A short what-does-this-fact-change graph before the verdict is a cheap structured prompt for the S5 Revise slot.

source: Allaway et al. (2023) Penguins Don't Fly: reasoning about generics through instantiations and exceptions (EACL)
finding: A constrained generator makes exceptions and instantiations for 650 generics. NLI labels between a generic and its exception are not a clean contradiction.
numbers: 18,859 exemplars for 653 generics; beats a GPT-3 baseline by 12.8 precision points. NLI filtering raises exception precision at P@1 from 0.632 to 0.839 (+20.7 points) and at P@5 from 0.616 to 0.790; instantiation precision unchanged (0.911 vs 0.864).
limits: Data-generation paper; the NLI view is a side analysis. The authors note that exception labels do not line up with NLI neatly (their Figure 3).
agent_relevance: Do not use an entailment checker to detect defeaters: many valid exceptions read as neutral.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors and Kemp (2023) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models
finding: GPT-4 matches human property-induction judgments on most phenomena. The one notable failure is premise non-monotonicity: adding a premise that lowers argument strength.
numbers: Human Exp 1 N=110 after excluding 10 who failed checks; Exp 2 humans saw 42 arguments each. Spearman 0.65 between a replication of Osherson et al. rankings and the originals. GPT-3.5 failed many phenomena; GPT-4 failed only premise non-monotonicity.
limits: Inductive (similarity) non-monotonicity, not default logic. Exact GPT-4 correlations not read.
agent_relevance: Models track more support, more belief well but not more evidence, less belief. That is the failure that matters for retraction.

source: Sadhu, Shahad and Marino (2026) DERELAB: defeasible reasoning and confirmation bias in LLMs
finding: Nine models fail to retract when a weakening update arrives. Many accept congruent evidence and resist incongruent evidence.
numbers: 900 multi-turn conversations, 18,390 turns, default and inheritance reasoning, formally verified ground truth. Confirmation-bias gap significant in 17 of 19 model-by-task cells (Holm-Bonferroni). GPT-5.1 gap 0.935 (OR 891, CI 586-1498); incongruent accuracy 3.5%. Gemma-4-12B gap 0.082. Default anchoring (kept first answer after the truth changed): GPT-5.1 0.433, Qwen3-32B 0.483.
limits: Nine models, 2026 vintage, synthetic entity graphs. Two cells not significant. Gaps depend on question order.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the model alone does not retract. Retraction should be done by code from a dependency record, not by asking the model.

source: Sadhu, Shahad and Marino (2026) DERELAB: know-but-do-not-output and question order
finding: Models often label an update as weakening correctly, yet keep the old conclusion on the same turn.
numbers: GPT-5-mini: weakening labelled correctly 95.4%, conclusion revised correctly only 20.3%. Llama-3.1-70B: 85.1% vs 14.9%. Reversing question order cut correct weakening labels sharply: Gemma-4-31B 0.970 to 0.264; Gemma-4-12B 0.887 to 0.209; Qwen3-32B 0.803 to 0.414.
limits: The effect label may be scaffolded by earlier answering, per the authors. Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Ask for the effect of the update first, then let code apply it to the conclusion. Do not trust a one-shot final answer after a defeater.

source: Sadhu, Shahad and Marino (2026) DERELAB: thinking mode and difficulty
finding: Extended thinking removed most of the bias in one model. Default reasoning was harder than inheritance.
numbers: Qwen3-32B with thinking: bias gap 0.008 (OR 1.07), anchoring 0.032 (default) and 0.004 (inheritance). Same model without thinking: gap 0.670 (0.816 with reversed question order). Overall accuracy: Qwen3-32B thinking 86.0, GPT-5-mini thinking 83.7, Gemma-4-31B 82.4, Gemma-4-12B 78.3, GPT-5.1 72.5, Llama-3.1-70B 53.2, Gemma-4-E4B 47.0. Correct-answer confidence falls with inference distance (Gemma-4-31B slope -0.298).
limits: Thinking helps Qwen here but Kirkpatrick found CoT hurts older models. Different tasks (multi-turn graphs vs single inference).
agent_relevance: Reasoning budget helps graph-structured retraction. It is a conditional benefit, so trigger it by a signal (G1), not by default.

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya, Ishii, He and Fung (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of Large Language Models Reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: 30 LMs were tested on whether they update or keep a conclusion after a third premise (additional requirement vs alternative cause). Most fail to update. Models good at updating often over-update.
numbers: Basic inference (premises 1-2): pretrained models above 6B reach 75%; instruction-tuned from 2.7B above 90%. Belief Update accuracy near 0% for most open models; at most about 50% on the balanced score (BREU). Llama-3 70B: update 10.99%, maintain 92.09%, BREU 51.54. Mixtral 8x22B: update 35.38%, maintain 36.57%, BREU 35.98.
limits: Items generated with GPT-4 from ATOMIC and checked by crowd labels (about 2K items). Modus tollens harder. Model labels in the appendix table were partly garbled, so only two models are named.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement of the update/maintain trade-off. Forcing doubt gains updates but loses stable answers: the number behind G1.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R: prompting, distractors and item type
finding: Chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve prompting did not fix belief revision. A third, unrelated premise lowered accuracy on items that should be kept.
numbers: CoT or plan-and-solve changed the balanced score by about 1 point on average; per-model update/maintain shifts varied by sign (Llama-3 70B CoT 12.57/89.40; Mixtral CoT 27.28/34.93). On 378 matched queries most models lost accuracy when the third premise was added though no change was needed. Mental-state items favoured maintain; modus tollens items showed higher update but lower maintain.
limits: Zero-shot prompts only. No tool or solver arm.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only fix is unlikely. Pair the model with a rule store and a code check of the disabling condition.

source: Tachmazidis, Batsakis and Antoniou (2024) Benchmarking Defeasible Reasoning with LLMs: initial experiments
finding: A small test of GPT-4o on defeasible-logic theories (chains, cycles, DAGs, priority levels). Chains and cycles were solved. Priority levels and some orderings failed.
numbers: 8 theories x 4 prompt variants. levels-(5) wrong in all 4 variants; levels(5) wrong in 2 of 4; dag(3,2) wrong in 1 of 4 (hallucinated a fact). Chain, strict chain, circle, circles, hierarchies correct in all variants.
limits: One model, one run per cell, hand-checked. Preliminary, not statistics.
agent_relevance: Conflict resolution by priority is the weak point, as in LogicBench priorities. Statement order changed answers: fix an order in the schema.

source: Elio and Pelletier (1993); Pelletier and Elio (1997, 2005), as cited by Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025)
finding: Humans often resist default inferences about individuals already known to violate another default, so textbook non-monotonic patterns are not all accepted by people.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary source.
limits: Original studies not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not score an agent against a logic textbook alone. Some formal default patterns are not what people endorse.

source: Oaksford and Chater (1998) and Politzer and Braine (1991), as cited by Schroyens et al. (2010): defeasibility versus non-monotonicity
finding: One view: everyday inference is non-monotonic, so classical logic fails as a theory of reasoning. Counter-view: a conclusion's truth is defeasible but the inference's validity is not, so there is no conflict.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Secondary citation from the introduction of the Schroyens paper.
agent_relevance: Design point: keep the rule-is-valid record separate from the conclusion-currently-held record. Retract the second without deleting the first.

source: Deveci et al. (2026) ArgGYM: a procedural benchmark for structured defeasible reasoning
finding: On 1,440 verified instances of structured defeasible reasoning, models recover parts of answers far more often than whole answers. More thinking helps but not evenly.
numbers: Complete-task success: best configuration 82.4% (Gemini 3.8 Flash, high effort); GPT-OSS-120B 12.4% (low) to 29.0% (high); Gemma-4-31B 14.4% to 27.3% with thinking; Qwen3.8-27B 28.4% to 39.2%. Local versus complete: Qwen3.5-27B 88.7 native vs 35.8% complete on status queries. Last-link versus weakest-link preference: Gemini 3.8 Flash 92.9% vs 71.8%; Qwen3.5-27B 50.1% vs 28.5%. Qwen3.8-27B strict-rule condition fell from 50.8% to 11.7% as effort rose.
limits: Preprint dated Sep 2026; model names could not be checked elsewhere. Formal task wording, not natural language.
agent_relevance: Partial credit hides failure: test the whole retraction chain, not each step. The preference rule changes scores by about 20 points, so fix it in the schema.
